fermentables.name: Apple Juice Concentrate
fermentables.description: Roughly 68 Brix — about six times the strength of single-strength juice.
fermentables.usageNotes: Reconstitute at about 1 part concentrate to 6 parts water for a normal cider gravity: 7 CFR 52.6322 grades 68 Brix as a six-to-one concentrate, not the five-to-one this record used to advise.
fermentables.attribution: Sugar is derived, not stored as Brix. The record previously set sugar equal to the 68 Brix concentration, which counts the concentrate's organic acid, pectin and minerals as fermentable sugar. USDA FoodData Central measures the gap for single-strength apple juice (SR Legacy, FDC ID 173933, Apple juice, canned or bottled, unsweetened): sugars are 81.8% of total solids there, so a 68 Brix concentrate carries about 55.6 g of sugar per 100 g, not 68. ppg is 46 x that. The minimum and maximum are the same conversion applied to the stored Brix range. The citation is the data endpoint rather than the portal page, which FDC serves from a client-side router and returns 404 to anything that is not a browser. The Brix concentration is graded: the United States Standards for Grades of Frozen Concentrated Apple Juice, section 52.6322, set the minimum Brix of the finished concentrate at each dilution factor - 22.9 degrees at 1 plus 1, then 33.0, 42.2, 50.8, 58.8, 66.3 and 73.3 at 7 plus 1. Issued by USDA's Agricultural Marketing Service under the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946, published at 40 FR 13195 and effective 15 May 1975.
fermentables.sourceNote:
The reconstitution advice on this record was wrong and the standard is what shows it. It said to reconstitute at about 1 part concentrate to 5 parts water, but section 52.6322 puts 68 Brix between the 6 plus 1 grade (minimum 66.3) and the 7 plus 1 grade (minimum 73.3), so a 68 Brix concentrate is a six-to-one product and diluting it five-to-one overshoots the gravity. The dilution factors are volumetric and the standard's own figures are not linear in Brix - 22.9 at 1 plus 1 against 73.3 at 7 plus 1 - because the concentrate is much denser than water, so do not interpolate them by hand.

Two limits on this citation. First, the standard is cited to the AMS document rather than to the Code of Federal Regulations, because it is no longer in the Code: 7 CFR part 52 now ends at section 52.3764 and the whole 52.6321-52.6332 subpart for frozen concentrated apple juice has been removed, so an eCFR link would be dead. AMS still publishes it as a voluntary grade standard and that PDF is what was read. Second, the standard grades Brix, which is soluble solids, and says nothing about how much of those solids is sugar; that conversion comes from USDA's measurement of the single-strength juice. Using the single-strength ratio is deliberately conservative - USDA's own concentrate record puts sugars at 90.3% of solids against 81.8% in the juice, so the true figure is likely a few grams higher than the 55.6 stored here. Titratable acidity, pH and pectin remain unsourced curation.

fermentables.name: Grape Juice Concentrate
fermentables.description: About 68 Brix. The standard body-and-sugar addition for kit wines and a common mead adjunct.
fermentables.usageNotes: Adds tartaric acid along with the sugar — account for it before making acid corrections.
fermentables.attribution: Sugar is derived, not stored as Brix. The record previously set sugar equal to the 68 Brix concentration, which counts the concentrate's organic acid, pectin and minerals as fermentable sugar. USDA FoodData Central measures the gap for single-strength grape juice (SR Legacy, FDC ID 173042, Grape juice, canned or bottled, unsweetened): sugars are 91.7% of total solids there, so a 68 Brix concentrate carries about 62.4 g of sugar per 100 g, not 68. ppg is 46 x that. The minimum and maximum are the same conversion applied to the stored Brix range. The citation is the data endpoint rather than the portal page, which FDC serves from a client-side router and returns 404 to anything that is not a browser.
fermentables.sourceNote: The 68 Brix concentration itself is not sourced. There is a US grade standard for frozen concentrated grape juice, 7 CFR 52.2453, but it governs *sweetened* concentrate - its Brix figures include added sweetening ingredient - so it cannot bound an unsweetened grape concentrate, and there is no AMS standard for tart cherry concentrate at all. 68 Brix is the commercial trade concentration rather than a graded one, and it is carried over from this project's earlier curation. What is sourced here is the conversion from that Brix to sugar. Note also that USDA measures the sugars-to-solids ratio rising as juice is concentrated - apple goes from 81.8% single-strength to 90.3% in USDA's own concentrate record - so applying the single-strength ratio makes this a conservative figure, low rather than high. Titratable acidity and pH remain unsourced.

fermentables.name: Orange Juice
fermentables.description: Ferments cleanly but loses most of its aroma; the result reads more like a dry citrus wine than orange juice.
fermentables.usageNotes: Pasteurised carton juice is reliable; check for added preservatives.
fermentables.attribution: Sugar is USDA FoodData Central's figure for Orange juice, canned, unsweetened (SR Legacy, FDC ID 169099): 8.76 g per 100 g, and ppg is 46 x that. FoodData Central marks it Analytical - measured, not estimated, from 3 samples, reported range 8.48-8.96 g per 100 g. The stored 11 was a quarter high. The citation is the data endpoint rather than the portal page, which FDC serves from a client-side router and returns 404 to anything that is not a browser.
fermentables.sourceNote: The canned record is cited rather than the obvious one. FDC ID 169098, "Orange juice, raw", is the record a search puts first and it carries 8.4 g of sugar, but USDA derives that one "Based on another form of the food or similar food" - it is imputed, not measured. The canned unsweetened juice is the only orange juice in SR Legacy whose sugar is Analytical, and the two figures agree to within 4%, so nothing is lost by preferring the measured one. Everything except sugar, ppg and the Codex Brix floor below is unsourced curation.

additionalSources.supports: Codex Alimentarius CXS 247-2005, General Standard for Fruit Juices and Nectars, Annex, sets the minimum Brix for reconstituted Orange juice at 10.0 (the Annex's absolute floor; the nominal figure is 11.8-11.2, but it admits juice down to 10 Brix from countries whose fruit runs consistently lower) at 20 C. The stored minimum of 10 already sits at or above that floor, so Codex bounds this record without changing it. The floor is a trade-authenticity minimum, not the lowest Brix ever measured in the fruit.

fermentables.name: Pineapple Juice
fermentables.description: Canned or carton juice is heat-treated, so the bromelain problem is already solved.
fermentables.usageNotes: Unlike fresh pineapple this will not attack gelatin or beer foam.
fermentables.attribution: Sugar is USDA FoodData Central's figure for Pineapple juice, canned or bottled, unsweetened, without added ascorbic acid (SR Legacy, FDC ID 169947): 9.98 g per 100 g, and ppg is 46 x that. FoodData Central marks it Analytical - measured, not estimated, from 1 sample. The stored 13 was 30% high. The citation is the data endpoint rather than the portal page, which FDC serves from a client-side router and returns 404 to anything that is not a browser.
fermentables.sourceNote: One sample, so the figure is a measurement but not a survey. USDA publishes no range for it, so the stored minimum is now that single measured value rather than a wider guess. Everything except sugar, ppg and the Codex Brix floor below is unsourced.

additionalSources.supports: Codex Alimentarius CXS 247-2005, General Standard for Fruit Juices and Nectars, Annex, sets the minimum Brix for reconstituted Pineapple juice at 10.0 (the Annex's absolute floor; the nominal figure is 12.8, but it admits juice down to 10 Brix from countries whose fruit runs consistently lower) at 20 C. The stored minimum of 12 already sits at or above that floor, so Codex bounds this record without changing it. The floor is a trade-authenticity minimum, not the lowest Brix ever measured in the fruit.

fermentables.name: Cranberry Juice (100%)
fermentables.description: Unsweetened cranberry juice is brutally acidic — most retail 'cranberry juice' is a sweetened cocktail at a fraction of the strength.
fermentables.usageNotes: Read the label: cocktail blends are typically 25% juice and already contain sugar.
fermentables.attribution: The Brix floor is Codex Alimentarius CXS 247-2005, General Standard for Fruit Juices and Nectars, Annex: the minimum Brix for reconstituted cranberry juice (Vaccinium macrocarpon Aiton, V. oxycoccos L.) is 7.5 at 20 C, and the stored minimum of 7 was below it. The sugar figure is not sourced - see below.
fermentables.sourceNote: USDA has a record for this and it was rejected. FDC ID 168117, "Cranberry juice, unsweetened", carries 12.1 g of sugar per 100 g, but USDA derives it by "Other procedure used from imputing" - no measurement, and its water content is imputed too. It also fails an independent check: 12.1 g of sugar in a juice USDA puts at 12.87 g of total solids would be roughly 12.9 Brix, and Codex sets authentic cranberry juice at a minimum of 7.5 Brix, with commercial single-strength juice sitting near that floor rather than at 13. Two sources cannot both be right and the one with no measurement behind it loses. SR Legacy has no analytical figure for pure unsweetened cranberry juice at all - every analytical cranberry entry in it is a sweetened cocktail or a blend - so the stored 7.5 g stands as unsourced curation, consistent with the Codex floor but not established by it.

additionalSources.supports: Codex Alimentarius CXS 247-2005, General Standard for Fruit Juices and Nectars, Annex, sets the minimum Brix for reconstituted Cranberry juice at 7.5 at 20 C. The stored minimum was 7, below that floor - juice at 7 Brix could not be sold as cranberry juice - so it has been raised to 7.5. This is a trade-authenticity floor, not the lowest Brix ever measured in the fruit.
